name: Bookan
confidence_why: No source states where stress falls in Bookan: Prentice 1971 describes penultimate stress only for Timugon, and his Baukan outline, which records only what differs from Timugon, says nothing about stress, while Spitzack 1984, Lobel 2013, Mahali and Wong 2022 and Mahali 2024 are silent, so any rule for Bookan would be an inference rather than a finding.
catalog_citation: Prentice, D. J. 1971. The Murut languages of Sabah. Pacific Linguistics C-18. Canberra: The Australian National University. xi+311 pp. doi:10.15144/PL-C18
catalog_locator: sec. 10.2.2 'The Baukan dialect', 10.2.2.1 Phonology, pp. 282-283 (PDF pp. 294-295; no stress statement; stress-marked Baukan forms [ámaku], [bəré:n] p. 282 and [liŋəŋé:t], [tətɔ́:n], [məpé:t], [né:tilan] p. 283); sec. 10.0 p. 274 (PDF p. 286; differences-only method of the outline studies); sec. 2.2.1-2.2.1.3 p. 14 (PDF p. 26; Timugon stress); sec. 2.3.3.3.1 and 2.3.4.1.2 (Timugon irregular stress and vowel-cluster stress); page renders (200 dpi) of printed pp. 14, 282, 283 under the copy we hold
catalog_quote: [p. 14, 2.2.1 STRESS, Timugon] Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure. ... 2.2.1.1 Strong stress. Strong stress (marked by ´) occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word (see also 2.3.4.1.2): /mamatoy/ [...] 'will kill' /potoyon/ [...] 'will be killed' [p. 274, 10.0] The descriptions are of necessity based on the detailed analysis of the Poros subdialect of Timugon already presented ... attention is focused mainly on those features which exhibit differences with Timugon. ... The next section gives an account of the phonology, including an inventory of phonemes and a description of any distributional or allophonic features which differ significantly from the Timugon pattern. [pp. 282-283, 10.2.2.1 Phonology, THE BAUKAN DIALECT] The phoneme inventory of Baukan consists of /p t k ʔ b d g m n ŋ s l r y w i u o a/. ... The glottal stop /ʔ/ is elided before a clitic pronoun or determiner, as in /amaʔ ku/ [ámaku] 'my father'. The most noticeable phonological feature of Baukan is that the sequences /au/ and /ai/ (but not /aw/ and /ay/) are always realised as [ɔ:] and [e:] respectively. Any /a/ in the syllable immediately preceding such a sequence is reduced to [ə] or even (between identical consonants) elided altogether. Thus: /gaiʔ/ [ge:ʔ] 'evening' /barain/ [bəré:n] 'S will inform T/R' /liŋaŋait/ [liŋəŋé:t] or [liŋŋé:t] 'scorpion' /daun/ [dɔ:n] 'leaf' /tataun/ [tətɔ́:n] or [ttɔ́:n] 'tree; wood' /mapait/ [məpé:t] 'T/S will be bitter' /naitilan/ [né:tilan] 'T/S was hungry' [10.2.2 contains no sentence about stress]
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (Prentice 1971, full scan with text layer) rendered to page images for PDF pp. 26, 286, 294-295 (= printed pp. 14, 274, 282-283), plus the excerpt copy (1) Verbatim: p. 14 sec. 2.2.1 reads exactly 'Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure.' and 2.2.1.1 'Strong stress (marked by an acute) occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word (see also 2.3.4.1.2)'; p. 274 sec. 10.0 reads exactly 'The next section gives an account of the phonology, including an inventory of phonemes and a description of any distributional or allophonic features which differ signific…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No Baukan-specific stress statement exists in any source opened. Prentice treats Baukan as a dialect of the Lowland Murut language (with Timugon and Nabay) and, in an outline that by his stated method lists only departures from Timugon phonology, reports none for stress; for Timugon he states non-phonemic word stress with strong stress on the penultimate syllable. Reading for Bookan = penultimate by implication only.
new_statements.secondary_stress: For Timugon (p. 14, 2.2.1.2): weak stress on the first syllable of the word when separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables (/pamamagambad/ 'camera'); weak stress also replaces strong stress in a word subordinate to another within a phrase. Nothing stated for Baukan.
new_statements.exceptions: For Timugon only: 2.3.3.3 a few words, particularly those ending in -aCa?, are stressed on the last syllable (kaga? 'very', madada? 'dislike', masaga? 'wish'); stress vs. vowel quantity (/taNkuN/ vs /taNkuuN/) and stress shifts within vowel clusters (rising diphthongs, 2.3.4). Baukan: /au ai/ monophthongise to long [o: e:] with reduction of the preceding /a/ (e.g. /tataun/ [tato:n] ~ [tto:n] 'tree'), which bears on where prominence sits but is not framed as a stress rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level strong stress, with phrase-level demotion to weak stress (Timugon). The Baukan data are from Tulid village, upper Sook river (informant Lingodow bin Ginadan); the penult reading is inherited from the language-level (Timugon, Poros subdialect) description, not observed for Baukan.
new_statements.identity_note: Prentice 1971 describes 'the Baukan dialect' of Lowland Murut from Tulid village on the upper Sook river (Keningau district); Spitzack 1984 splits the Baukan language into Baukan proper and Tengara dialects. Glottolog book1241 Bookan [bnb] sits under Lowland Murut together with Timugon Murut (timu1262) and Keningau Murut/Nabay; the explicit penult-stress statement quoted is for Timugon (Poros subdialect, timu1262), not for Bookan itself.
